title_en:
Akamai, a $12B company, built a SECOND version of its website that only AI agents could see.

its AI search visibility increased 364%, while citations jumped 85%.

here's the genius AEO system behind it:

/1 They realized AI wasn't reading their website the same way humans did

-> Akamai operates a massive website covering cybersecurity, cloud computing, and developer infrastructure.

-> but its content wasn't consistently appearing when people asked AI about the products it offered.

-> their team believed part of the problem was how AI agents were accessing and interpreting those pages.

/2 So they built TWO versions of the same website

-> when a normal person visited Akamai, they saw the regular website, with its design, navigation, and interactive elements.

-> but when a supported AI agent requested a page, Akamai's system delivered a different, simplified version.

-> same URL, same underlying product information, but without the extra code, menus, and other elements AI didn't need.

/3 They made it work automatically through their CDN

-> Akamai used its edge infrastructure to identify incoming AI traffic before the requests reached its website.

-> detected AI agents were routed through Scrunch's Agent Experience Platform, which delivered simpler HTML versions of Akamai's existing content.

-> unlike llms.txt (which major AI search engines don't reliably read), this approach delivers optimized content directly when supported AI agents request a page.

-> they didn't have to redesign their public website or manually rewrite every page.

/4 They removed unnecessary code from the pages AI received

-> modern websites contain a lot more than the information visitors actually need: JavaScript, navigation, interactive elements, and other code.

-> Scrunch produced machine-readable versions using Akamai's existing product pages and documentation.

-> the goal was to make the information easier for AI to retrieve and understand, without changing what human visitors saw.

/5 They didn't roll it out across the entire website immediately

-> the first test focused on pages related to Akamai's Inference Cloud offering.

-> they measured how these pages appeared across selected AI prompts before optimization.

-> then they compared pages receiving the optimized treatment against pages that weren't.

/6 The first results were pretty significant

-> optimized pages received 85% more total AI citations.

-> they were cited across 38% more unique prompts.

-> brand visibility for questions that DIDN'T mention Akamai by name increased 364%.

-> in ChatGPT, Akamai's brand presence against competitors improved 133%.

and this last point is especially important.

people weren't just asking "what is Akamai?" and getting Akamai's website back.

the company started appearing more often when buyers asked general questions about the problems its products solve.

/7 The company decided to expand the system

-> after the initial test, Akamai began rolling the approach out across more of its website.

-> it also turned the technology into a commercial product called AI Brand Presence.

-> the same infrastructure it uses to manage web traffic could now detect AI agents, change how they receive content, and measure the results.

Akamai essentially built a system where humans and AI receive different versions of the same underlying website information.

and in its initial test, that was associated with a 364% improvement in visibility for searches where people weren't even mentioning the brand.

if you want to rank #1 on AI search + turn AI traffic into pileline,

full_text_zh:
Akamai 是一家价值 120 亿美元的公司，构建了只有人工智能代理才能看到的第二个版本的网站。

其 AI 搜索可见度增加了 364%，引用量猛增 85%。

这是其背后的天才 AEO 系统：

/1 他们意识到人工智能并没有像人类那样阅读他们的网站

-> Akamai 运营着一个涵盖网络安全、云计算和开发人员基础设施的大型网站。

-> 但当人们向 AI 询问其提供的产品时，其内容并没有始终如一地出现。

-> 他们的团队认为部分问题在于人工智能代理如何访问和解释这些页面。

/2 所以他们建立了同一网站的两个版本

-> 当普通人访问 Akamai 时，他们会看到常规网站及其设计、导航和交互元素。

-> 但当受支持的 AI 代理请求页面时，Akamai 的系统会提供不同的简化版本。

-> 相同的 URL、相同的基础产品信息，但没有额外的代码、菜单和其他人工智能不需要的元素。

/3 他们通过 CDN 使其自动运行

-> Akamai 使用其边缘基础设施在请求到达其网站之前识别传入的 AI 流量。

-> 检测到的 AI 代理通过 Scrunch 的代理体验平台进行路由，该平台提供 Akamai 现有内容的更简单的 HTML 版本。

-> 与 llms.txt（主要 AI 搜索引擎无法可靠读取）不同，这种方法在受支持的 AI 代理请求页面时直接提供优化的内容。

-> 他们不必重新设计他们的公共网站或手动重写每个页面。

/4 他们从 AI 收到的页面中删除了不必要的代码

-> 现代网站包含的信息远多于访问者实际需要的信息：JavaScript、导航、交互元素和其他代码。

-> Scrunch 使用 Akamai 现有的产品页面和文档制作了机器可读版本。

-> 目标是让人工智能更容易检索和理解信息，而不改变人类访问者所看到的内容。

/5 他们没有立即在整个网站上推广它

-> 第一个测试重点关注与 Akamai 推理云产品相关的页面。

-> 他们在优化之前测量了这些页面在选定的人工智能提示中的显示方式。

-> 然后他们将接受优化处理的页面与未接受优化处理的页面进行比较。

/6 第一个结果非常重要

-> 优化页面的 AI 总引用量增加了 85%。

-> 它们在独特提示中被引用的比例增加了 38%。

-> 对于未提及 Akamai 名称的问题，品牌知名度提高了 364%。

-> 在 ChatGPT 中，Akamai 相对于竞争对手的品牌影响力提高了 133%。

最后一点尤其重要。

人们不只是问“Akamai 是什么？”并恢复 Akamai 的网站。

当买家询问有关其产品解决的问题的一般性问题时，该公司开始更频繁地出现。

/7 公司决定扩展系统

-> 初步测试后，Akamai 开始在其网站的更多区域推广该方法。

-> 它还将该技术转化为一种名为 AI Brand Presence 的商业产品。

-> 用于管理网络流量的相同基础设施现在可以检测人工智能代理，改变它们接收内容的方式并测量结果。

Akamai 本质上构建了一个系统，人类和人工智能可以接收同一基础网站信息的不同版本。

在最初的测试中，人们甚至没有提及该品牌的搜索可见度提高了 364%。

如果你想在AI搜索上排名第一+将AI流量转化为桩线，

回复“GTA”

title_en:
I’ve watched plenty of AI agent demos that looked amazing. I wouldn’t trust any of them with my wallet.

That gap is what i keep coming back to. Imagine actually hiring an agent today, and count how many things could go wrong.

You can’t tell if it’s real. The name, bio, and “past work” can all be copied. A bad agent can disappear and return under a new name with a clean record.

You can’t check if it can do the job. There’s no history, just a pitch.

Payment is awkward either way. Pay first and you’re hoping. Pay after and the agent is hoping.

Nobody verifies the work. “Done” is just a word, and if you disagree, there’s no one to ask.

And there’s no record afterward. The next client walks into the same mess.

That’s fine for a demo. It breaks the moment agents work for money, and especially when agents start hiring other agents, because no human is there to catch the mistakes.

So i don’t see identity, reputation, and escrow as nice extras. They’re the minimum for an agent economy to exist at all. Humans built whole industries around them, and agents will need the same.

@termix_ai is building this layer. What I’ll be watching is whether it holds up under real jobs.

What’s the one thing an agent would need to show you before you’d let it handle real money?

full_text_en:
I’ve watched plenty of AI agent demos that looked amazing. I wouldn’t trust any of them with my wallet.

That gap is what i keep coming back to. Imagine actually hiring an agent today, and count how many things could go wrong.

You can’t tell if it’s real. The name, bio, and “past work” can all be copied. A bad agent can disappear and return under a new name with a clean record.

You can’t check if it can do the job. There’s no history, just a pitch.

Payment is awkward either way. Pay first and you’re hoping. Pay after and the agent is hoping.

Nobody verifies the work. “Done” is just a word, and if you disagree, there’s no one to ask.

And there’s no record afterward. The next client walks into the same mess.

That’s fine for a demo. It breaks the moment agents work for money, and especially when agents start hiring other agents, because no human is there to catch the mistakes.

So i don’t see identity, reputation, and escrow as nice extras. They’re the minimum for an agent economy to exist at all. Humans built whole industries around them, and agents will need the same.

@termix_ai is building this layer. What I’ll be watching is whether it holds up under real jobs.

full_text_zh:
我看过很多看起来很棒的人工智能代理演示。我不会相信他们中的任何一个人会用我的钱包。

这个差距是我不断回想起的。想象一下今天实际雇用一名代理人，并计算一下有多少事情可能会出错。

你无法判断它是否真实。姓名、简历和“过去的工作”都可以复制。不良代理人可能会消失，然后以新的名字和干净的记录重新出现。

你无法检查它是否能完成这项工作。没有历史，只有一个球场。

无论哪种方式付款都很尴尬。先付款，你就满怀希望了。付款后，代理希望。

没有人验证工作。 “完成”只是一个词，如果你不同意，也没有人可以问。

而且之后就没有任何记录了。下一个客户也陷入了同样的困境。

对于演示来说这很好。它打破了代理人为金钱而工作的那一刻，尤其是当代理人开始雇用其他代理人时，因为没有人可以发现错误。

所以我不认为身份、声誉和托管是额外的好处。它们是代理经济存在的最低限度。人类围绕它们建立了整个行业，代理商也需要同样的东西。

@termix_ai 正在构建这一层。我将关注的是它是否适用于实际工作。

title: When we pick a new gearbox for a kiln drive, the spec sheet isn't the first thing we look at. The first question is how
title_en:
When we pick a new gearbox for a kiln drive, the spec sheet isn't the first thing we look at. The first question is how many plants have run that exact model, and for how many years.

Edgars' article on the @GenLayer chain moving to @arbitrum Nitro makes the same call.

Nitro has years of production use behind it. Its core is Geth, Ethereum's most widely used client. It isn't a new design GenLayer has to prove first.

That matters more for GenLayer than for most chains. The chain holds the history of every GenLayer verdict, and a verdict is only as trustworthy as the record it sits on.

You don't put an untested gearbox on a kiln that runs all year. You don't put a court's record on an untested chain either.

If you were building on GenLayer, would you trust its verdicts more on a stack with years in production, or one built fresh for it?

title:
this is the Citadel trading algorithm that got them fined by the SEC & cost them $22.6M... 

it's absolutely DANGEROUS
title_en:
this is the Citadel trading algorithm that got them fined by the SEC & cost them $22.6M... 

it's absolutely DANGEROUS

it's called FastFill - when Citadel Securities' direct feeds already showed a better price, it filled retail orders off the worse public quote, about 2.7 MILLION times

the SEC's bill: $16M fine + $5.2M disgorgement + $1.47M interest = $22,665,268

i rebuilt it rule by rule from the SEC's own text, together with its sister algorithm SmartProvide, & replayed 20 minutes of LIVE BTC order books from 4 exchanges: FastFill fired on 1,273 of 2,267 orders

first understand how it worked:

> the exchanges' direct feeds show every displayed order first, the public quote counts only round lots & lands MILLISECONDS later

> FastFill: the SEC's own example is a buy filled at $10.01 while the direct feeds already showed $10.00. the order often got a sliver of improvement, but it often didn't close the gap

> SmartProvide: when the public quote beat a direct feed, the order wasn't filled at that price. it was displayed in the market for up to 1 to 5 seconds instead, about 690,000 orders

how to run it yourself with Claude Code/Grok Bot:

1. open Claude Code/Grok Bot & tell it to clone https://t.co/p5IBYiq4q6 & read AGENTS. md

2. have it run pip install -e . inside the folder, no API keys needed

3. have it run citadel-fastfill live & watch every FastFill & SmartProvide fire on BTC as it happens

4. have it run citadel-fastfill record --minutes 20 --out data/run1 to save the order books of Coinbase, Kraken, Bitstamp & Gemini

5. have it run citadel-fastfill replay --data data/run1 & read your numbers right next to the SEC's

6. ask it to explain ANY single order & it walks you through every step with the SEC paragraph behind it

7. have it run citadel-fastfill sensitivity --data data/run1 & see what changes when the public quote lags anywhere from 0.5 ms to 1,000 ms

8. ask it to add the exchange you actually trade on

9. record the books while you trade, then have it run citadel-fastfill markout --fills my_fills.csv --data data/run1 & see if price moved against YOU right after your fills

i won't say anything more:

它被称为 FastFill - 当 Citadel 证券的直接馈送已经显示出更好的价格时，它会从最差的公开报价中填充零售订单，大约 270 万次

SEC 的法案：1600 万美元罚款 + 520 万美元非法所得 + 147 万美元利息 = 22,665,268 美元

我根据 SEC 自己的文本及其姊妹算法 SmartProvide 逐条重建了它，并重播了 4 个交易所的 20 分钟实时 BTC 订单簿：FastFill 触发了 2,267 个订单中的 1,273 个订单

首先了解它是如何工作的：

> 交易所的直接提要首先显示每个显示的订单，公开报价仅计算整手数并在几毫秒后落地

> FastFill：SEC 自己的例子是以 10.01 美元成交，而直接反馈已经显示 10.00 美元。订单经常会得到一点点改善，但往往并不能缩小差距

> SmartProvide：当公开报价超过直接报价时，订单不会以该价格成交。相反，它在市场上展示的时间长达1到5秒，大约有69万个订单

如何使用 Claude Code/Grok Bot 自行运行：

1. 打开 Claude Code/Grok Bot 并告诉它克隆 并读取 AGENTS。 MD

2.运行 pip install -e 。在文件夹内，不需要 API 密钥

3.让它实时运行 citadel-fastfill 并观察 BTC 上发生的每一次 FastFill 和 SmartProvide 火灾

4. 运行 citadel-fastfill record -- 分钟 20 --out data/run1 来保存 Coinbase、Kraken、Bitstamp 和 Gemini 的订单簿

5.让它运行 citadel-fastfill replay --data data/run1 并读取 SEC 旁边的数字

6. 要求它解释任何单个订单，它会引导您完成每一步，并在后面附有 SEC 段落

7. 让它运行 citadel-fastfillsensitivity --data data/run1 并查看当公开报价滞后 0.5 毫秒到 1,000 毫秒时会发生什么变化

8.要求它添加您实际交易的交易所

9. 在交易时记录账簿，然后让它运行 citadel-fastfill markout --fills my_fills.csv --data data/run1 并查看成交后价格是否对您不利

title:

title_en:
Anthropic just killed API keys... FINALLY!

They just introduced Claude Platform OAuth, and this opens up some interesting possibilities for AI agent platforms

Here's what it enables:

- Users connect their Claude organization through OAuth. No API keys to share

- API usage is billed directly to the customer's organization

- Developers can choose who pays for each API request

- Users can set spending limits and revoke access anytime

- Platforms can focus on building agents and workflows instead of managing customer API keys

I'm already working on integrating this into https://t.co/pEjytZiAFd

Imagine browsing a catalog of agents, skills, and components, and running them directly with your own Claude organization

No API keys to copy, no complicated setup

This could change how we build and distribute AI agents 🤩

The entire authorization flow is explained in this diagram 👇

full_text_zh:
Anthropic 刚刚杀死了 API 密钥...终于！

他们刚刚推出了 Claude Platform OAuth，这为 AI 代理平台带来了一些有趣的可能性

以下是它的功能：

- 用户通过 OAuth 连接他们的 Claude 组织。没有可共享的 API 密钥

- API 使用量直接向客户组织计费

- 开发者可以选择谁为每个 API 请求付费

- 用户可以随时设置支出限额并撤销访问权限

- 平台可以专注于构建代理和工作流程，而不是管理客户 API 密钥

无需复制 API 密钥，无需复杂的设置

这可能会改变我们构建和分发人工智能代理的方式🤩

title:
If you're worried about A.I., you should think about the tractor. 

Yes, the tractor. 👇

An Iowa inventor named John Fro
title_en:
If you're worried about A.I., you should think about the tractor. 

Yes, the tractor. 👇

An Iowa inventor named John Froelich built the first practical gasoline tractor in 1892. Froelich left the business, but the firm, renamed the Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company, went on to build the Waterloo Boy: a two-cylinder kerosene tractor. But that's not what really changed the world. 

Ford changed the world. 

As he’d done with cars, Henry Ford perfected the tractor. Ford’s tractor debuted in October 1917 at $750, or roughly $137,000 today. In March 1918, John Deere bought the Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company. The John Deere Model D arrived in 1923, stayed in production for 30 years, and sold 160,000 units. Anticipating the competition, in February 1922, Ford cut the price of his tractor to $395. The industry called what followed the “tractor wars.” 

In 1923 alone, Ford built more than 100,000 tractors.

The resulting vast increase to farming productivity was probably the single biggest, most important fundamental economic change in human history to that point. 

In 1830, growing 100 bushels of wheat took 250 to 300 hours of human labor with a walking plow, a sickle, and a flail. By 1930, with a tractor, a gang plow, and a combine, the same 100 bushels took 15 to 20 hours, a 95% reduction.

In 1920, American farms owned 246,083 tractors and 25.2 million horses and mules. By 1950, they owned 3.25 million tractors and only 7.6 million horses and mules. I bet you've never thought about how much that changed -- or created -- the modern world. 

A mature farm horse needed about three acres of cropland for feed every year. At “peak horse” in 1915, roughly 93 million acres of American cropland grew food for horses and mules rather than for people.

The economic historians Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode calculated that the tractor replaced 23 million draft animals between 1910 and 1960. That added 79 million acres to the effective cropland base, an area equal to two-thirds of all the cropland harvested across the Louisiana Purchase.

By 1960, the tractor cut the labor needed to grow America’s crops by about 1.7 million workers.

So who lost? The horse breeders lost, and so did the oat growers who fed the horses. The harness makers, the livery stables, and the farm blacksmiths lost too. And, of course, millions of farmers who didn’t take advantage of the new machinery and vastly expand their acreage also lost.

But… who won? America won. All of us.

In 1900, 41% of America’s workforce worked in agriculture. By 1930, the share was 21.5%, and by 2000, it was only 1.9%.

It was this fundamental change to farming productivity that created our cities. The 1920 census was the first in our history to count more Americans in towns and cities than in the countryside: 51.2%. During the 1920s, for the first time in our history, the total rural population actually fell.

So… what happened to the farmers? They followed prices (wages) to build what the economy needed. It didn’t need farmers anymore, thanks to tractors. The new economy needed cars and radios, city offices, stores, and hospitals. While they went on to build these things (and invent many others), the food they no longer had to grow kept arriving from fewer farms, at lower prices.

But hang on, didn’t the advent of the tractor and the changes to farming cause the Great Depression? Remember the “Okies”? Remember John Steinbeck’s The Grapes of Wrath?

For the farmers who couldn’t compete in the new world of tractor farming, politics held out the siren song of getting something for nothing. And getting disaffected farmers’ votes was a winning political strategy for decades. 

When Herbert Hoover became the U.S. president in March 1929, he called Congress into special session to deliver “farm relief through limited changes in the tariff.”

Much like President Trump today, Hoover believed tariffs were taxes that Americans wouldn’t have to pay. Those revenues could be used to give money to farmers. Congress took Hoover’s farm bill and loaded it with protection for thousands of other businesses.

More than 1,000 American economists signed a petition begging Hoover to veto the bill. They warned “the vast majority of farmers would also lose.” Henry Ford, the man selling tractors to those farmers, spent an evening at the White House calling the bill “an economic stupidity.” But Hoover signed it anyway, on June 17, 1930.

The Smoot-Hawley Tariff did exactly what the economists predicted. Canada retaliated before the bill was even signed, and Europe followed. Our exports fell from $5.24 billion in 1929 to $1.67 billion in 1933: a 68% collapse.

From 1926 through 1929, trade accounted for 15% to 17% of American farm income. It went to zero after the tariff. Farm-state banks failed by the thousands. Between December 1930 and March 1933, about half of all American banks either closed or merged.

But the tractor didn’t cause the Great Depression.

The productivity – the enormous wealth – it delivered was real. What turned that productivity into misery was government: a tariff wall that kept American farmers from selling their incredible abundance to the world.

And that's the big risk today. 

A big part of what’s driving the  angst and the political resistance to artificial intelligence (“AI”) is the computer nerds (who don't understand the first thing about economics) saying that humans will never have a job again.

Nonsense.

Yes, millions of jobs will vanish. Yes, whole trades will die. Yes, prices for things like legal work, accounting, and medical diagnosis will collapse. And yes, the capital invested in the old way of doing those things will get wiped out. People aren’t going to use Google’s web search anymore. 

But that doesn’t mean that Alphabet (GOOG) is going to go out of business.

Why not? Because creative destruction isn’t a flaw of capitalism – it’s the main feature.

Joseph Schumpeter, the Austrian economist, first explained all of this formally in 1942. But you still won’t see this taught in government schools. 

While Marx invented the term “creative destruction,” Schumpeter correctly explained it for the first time as a process that “incessantly revolutionizes the economic structure from within, incessantly destroying the old one, incessantly creating a new one.” He wrote that
“This process of Creative Destruction is the essential fact about capitalism,” and he described capitalism itself as “the perennial gale of creative destruction.”

The logic is simple. A new machine lets fewer people produce more, so prices fall. The workers and the capital that the old method no longer needs are set free, and prices tell them where they are needed next. The market allows them to go on to build new industries that nobody could have planned.

That’s why the AI nerds believe there won’t be any new jobs: they haven’t been created yet. 

Ironically, the AI that the nerds do understand is what will empower the human creativity and ingenuity that will build these entire new industries – if the government doesn’t get in the way.

Capitalism is the best way to organize a society and allocate its scarce resources for exactly this reason: it encourages creative destruction instead of preventing it. On the other hand, systems that protect incumbents stagnate. They don’t grow. They restrain human ingenuity. Poverty is the result.

We are living through a new huge “gale” of creative destruction today with AI. The temptation to stop it politically will be immense. And whether or not we – as a society – thrive or are destroyed by AI will depend on Americans continuing to choose freedom and capitalism over statism and poverty.

Given our changing demographics and the rise of communism in America, I’m honestly not optimistic. (And by the way, much of the blame for that rests with the Republicans who continue to pursue statist, big-government policies.)

The tractor of the AI age is the Nvidia (NVDA) accelerator chip: the machine that lets a small number of people do work that once took armies of them. I expect the creative destruction it unleashes to be every bit as violent as the tractor’s. And Washington has decided that the best way for us to manage it is to keep the machine at home.

The United States began restricting Nvidia’s advanced chips to China in 2022, and it still bans the export of Nvidia’s newest Blackwell and Rubin chips there. In December 2025, the White House allowed sales of the older H200 chips to approved Chinese buyers on one condition: the chips had to be routed through the United States, where the government collected a 25% tariff on the way out.

The barriers keep spreading. On Monday, the Commerce Department issued a rule requiring an export license to ship advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

We shouldn't fear AI. It's here. There's no putting the genie back in the bottle. And erecting barriers to trade is exactly what caused a great depression when the tractor arrived. 

Let's not make that mistake twice.

full_text_zh:
如果你担心人工智能，你应该考虑一下拖拉机。

是的，拖拉机。

爱荷华州的发明家约翰·弗罗利希 (John Froelich) 于 1892 年制造了第一台实用的汽油拖拉机。弗罗利希离开了公司，但公司更名为滑铁卢汽油发动机公司，继续制造滑铁卢男孩：一种两缸煤油拖拉机。但这并不是真正改变世界的原因。

福特改变了世界。

正如他对汽车所做的那样，亨利·福特完善了拖拉机。福特拖拉机于 1917 年 10 月首次亮相，售价为 750 美元，相当于今天的 137,000 美元左右。 1918 年 3 月，约翰迪尔收购了滑铁卢汽油发动机公司。约翰迪尔 Model D 于 1923 年问世，持续生产 30 年，销量达 160,000 辆。 1922 年 2 月，福特预见到了竞争，将拖拉机的价格降至 395 美元。业界将随后发生的事情称为“拖拉机大战”。

仅 1923 年一年，福特就生产了超过 100,000 辆拖拉机。

由此产生的农业生产力的大幅提高可能是迄今为止人类历史上最大、最重要的根本性经济变革。

1830 年，种植 100 蒲式耳小麦需要 250 至 300 个小时的人力，使用步行犁、镰刀和连枷。到 1930 年，使用拖拉机、群犁和联合收割机，同样的 100 蒲式耳需要 15 到 20 小时，减少了 95%。

1920年，美国农场拥有246,083台拖拉机和2520万匹马和骡子。到1950年，他们拥有325万辆拖拉机，只有760万匹马和骡子。我敢打赌你从来没有想过这改变了——或者创造了——现代世界。

一匹成熟的农马每年需要大约三英亩的耕地作为饲料。 1915 年的“马高峰”时期，大约 9300 万英亩的美国农田为马和骡子种植食物，而不是为人提供食物。

经济历史学家艾伦·奥姆斯特德和保罗·罗德计算出，1910 年至 1960 年间，拖拉机取代了 2300 万头役畜。这使得有效农田基地增加了 7900 万英亩，相当于路易斯安那购地期间收获的农田总面积的三分之二。

到 1960 年，拖拉机使美国种植农作物所需的劳动力减少了约 170 万人。

那么谁输了呢？马饲养者输了，喂养马的燕麦种植者也输了。马具制造商、马厩和农场铁匠也输了。当然，数百万没有利用新机械并大幅扩大种植面积的农民也遭受了损失。

但是……谁赢了？美国赢了。我们所有人。

1900 年，41% 的美国劳动力从事农业。到1930年，这一比例为21.5%，到2000年，仅为1.9%。

正是农业生产力的根本性变化创造了我们的城市。 1920 年的人口普查是我们历史上第一次统计出居住在城镇的美国人多于居住在农村的美国人：51.2%。 20 年代，农村人口总数实际上出现下降，这在我国历史上尚属首次。

那么……农民们怎么了？他们遵循价格（工资）来建设经济所需的东西。多亏了拖拉机，它不再需要农民了。新经济需要汽车和收音机、城市办公室、商店和医院。当他们继续建造这些东西（并发明了许多其他东西）时，他们不再需要种植的食物不断从更少的农场以更低的价格运来。

但等一下，拖拉机的出现和农业的变革不是导致了大萧条吗？还记得“奥基斯”吗？还记得约翰·斯坦贝克的《愤怒的葡萄》吗？

对于那些无法在拖拉机农业新世界中竞争的农民来说，政治提供了不劳而获的诱惑。几十年来，获得心怀不满的农民选票一直是一项获胜的政治策略。

1929 年 3 月，赫伯特·胡佛 (Herbert Hoover) 就任美国总统，他召集国会召开特别会议，“通过有限的关税变化来提供农业救济”。

就像今天的特朗普总统一样，胡佛认为关税是美国人不必缴纳的税款。这些收入可以用来给农民钱。国会采纳了胡佛的农业法案，并为数千家其他企业提供了保护。

1000多名美国经济学家签署了一份请愿书，请求胡佛否决该法案。他们警告说，“绝大多数农民也会遭受损失。”向这些农民出售拖拉机的亨利·福特在白宫度过了一个晚上，称该法案是“经济上的愚蠢行为”。但胡佛还是在 1930 年 6 月 17 日签署了该协议。

斯穆特-霍利关税完全符合经济学家的预测。加拿大在该法案签署之前就进行了报复，欧洲也紧随其后。我们的出口从 1929 年的 52.4 亿美元下降到 1933 年的 16.7 亿美元：下降了 68%。

从1926年到1929年，贸易占美国农业收入的15%到17%。关税之后它就降为零了。数以千计的农场国有银行倒闭。 1930 年 12 月至 1933 年 3 月期间，大约一半的美国银行关闭或合并。

但拖拉机并没有引发大萧条。

它带来的生产力——巨大的财富——是真实的。使生产力变成痛苦的是政府：关税墙阻止美国农民向世界出售其令人难以置信的丰富产品。

这就是今天的巨大风险。

引发对人工智能（“AI”）的焦虑和政治抵制的一个重要原因是计算机迷（他们对经济学一无所知）说人类将永远不会再有工作。

废话。

是的，数以百万计的工作岗位将会消失。是的，整个行业都会消亡。是的，法律工作、会计和医疗诊断等工作的价格将会崩溃。是的，以旧方式做这些事情所投入的资本将会被消灭。人们将不再使用谷歌的网络搜索。

但这并不意味着 Alphabet (GOOG) 将倒闭。

为什么不呢？因为创造性破坏不是资本主义的缺陷——它是主要特征。

奥地利经济学家约瑟夫·熊彼特 (Joseph Schumpeter) 在 1942 年首次正式解释了这一切。但你仍然不会在公立学校看到这些内容。

马克思发明了“创造性破坏”这个词，熊彼特第一次正确地将其解释为“不断地从内部彻底改变经济结构，不断地摧毁旧的经济结构，不断地创造新的经济结构”的过程。他写道
“这种创造性破坏的过程是资本主义的本质事实”，他将资本主义本身描述为“创造性破坏的常年狂风”。

逻辑很简单。新机器可以让更少的人生产更多的东西，因此价格下降。旧方法不再需要的工人和资本被释放，价格告诉他们下一步需要他们。市场使他们能够继续建立无人能计划的新产业。

这就是为什么人工智能迷相信不会有任何新的工作岗位：它们还没有被创造出来。

具有讽刺意味的是，如果政府不阻止的话，书呆子们真正理解的人工智能将增强人类的创造力和独创性，从而建立这些全新的产业。

资本主义是组织一个社会和分配其稀缺资源的最佳方式，正是因为这个原因：它鼓励创造性破坏，而不是阻止创造性破坏。另一方面，保护现有企业的制度停滞不前。它们不会生长。它们限制了人类的聪明才智。贫穷就是结果。

今天，我们正经历着人工智能带来的一场新的巨大的创造性破坏“风暴”。从政治上阻止它的诱惑将是巨大的。无论我们——作为一个社会——繁荣还是被人工智能摧毁，都将取决于美国人继续选择自由和资本主义，而不是国家主义和贫困。

考虑到我们不断变化的人口结构和美国共产主义的崛起，老实说我并不乐观。 （顺便说一句，这很大程度上要归咎于继续奉行集权主义、大政府政策的共和党人。）

人工智能时代的拖拉机是英伟达 (NVDA) 加速器芯片：这种机器可以让少数人完成曾经需要大量人员完成的工作。我预计它所释放的创造性破坏会像拖拉机一样暴力。华盛顿已经决定，我们管理它的最佳方法是将机器留在家里。

美国从2022年开始限制英伟达的先进芯片向中国出口，并且仍然禁止英伟达最新的Blackwell和Rubin芯片向中国出口。 2025 年 12 月，白宫允许向批准的中国买家销售较旧的 H200 芯片，但有一个条件：这些芯片必须经过美国，美国政府在出口时征收 25% 的关税。

障碍不断蔓延。周一，美国商务部发布了一项规定，要求向印度尼西亚、马来西亚、新加坡、泰国和巴西运送先进芯片需要获得出口许可证。

我们不应该害怕人工智能。就在这里。没有办法把精灵放回瓶子里。建立贸易壁垒正是拖拉机到来时造成大萧条的原因。

我们不要再犯同样的错误了。

滑铁卢男孩：一种两缸煤油拖拉机。但这并不是真正改变世界的原因。

福特改变了世界。

正如他对汽车所做的那样，亨利·福特完善了拖拉机。福特拖拉机于 1917 年 10 月首次亮相，售价为 750 美元，相当于今天的 137,000 美元左右。 1918 年 3 月，约翰迪尔收购了滑铁卢汽油发动机公司。约翰迪尔 Model D 于 1923 年问世，持续生产 30 年，销量达 160,000 辆。 1922 年 2 月，福特预见到了竞争，将拖拉机的价格降至 395 美元。业界将随后发生的事情称为“拖拉机大战”。

仅 1923 年一年，福特就生产了超过 100,000 辆拖拉机。

由此产生的农业生产力的大幅提高可能是迄今为止人类历史上最大、最重要的根本性经济变革。

1830 年，种植 100 蒲式耳小麦需要 250 至 300 个小时的人力，使用步行犁、镰刀和连枷。到 1930 年，使用拖拉机、群犁和联合收割机，同样的 100 蒲式耳需要 15 到 20 小时，减少了 95%。

1920年，美国农场拥有246,083台拖拉机和2520万匹马和骡子。到1950年，他们拥有325万辆拖拉机，只有760万匹马和骡子。我敢打赌你从来没有想过这改变了——或者创造了——现代世界。

一匹成熟的农马每年需要大约三英亩的耕地作为饲料。 1915 年的“马高峰”时期，大约 9300 万英亩的美国农田为马和骡子种植食物，而不是为人提供食物。

经济历史学家艾伦·奥姆斯特德和保罗·罗德计算出，1910 年至 1960 年间，拖拉机取代了 2300 万头役畜。这使得有效农田基地增加了 7900 万英亩，相当于路易斯安那购地期间收获的农田总面积的三分之二。

到 1960 年，拖拉机使美国种植农作物所需的劳动力减少了约 170 万人。

那么谁输了呢？马饲养者输了，喂养马的燕麦种植者也输了。马具制造商、马厩和农场铁匠也输了。当然，数百万没有利用新机械并大幅扩大种植面积的农民也遭受了损失。

但是……谁赢了？美国赢了。我们所有人。

1900 年，41% 的美国劳动力从事农业。到1930年，这一比例为21.5%，到2000年，仅为1.9%。

正是农业生产力的根本性变化创造了我们的城市。 1920 年的人口普查是我们历史上第一次统计出居住在城镇的美国人多于居住在农村的美国人：51.2%。 20 年代，农村人口总数实际上出现下降，这在我国历史上尚属首次。

那么……农民们怎么了？他们遵循价格（工资）来建设经济所需的东西。多亏了拖拉机，它不再需要农民了。新经济需要汽车和收音机、城市办公室、商店和医院。当他们继续建造这些东西（并发明了许多其他东西）时，他们不再需要种植的食物不断从更少的农场以更低的价格运来。

title_en:
THE MARKET HAS $NVDA COMPLETELY WRONG

I think that most investors believe that AI infrastructure spending is peaking and that therefore, Nvidia's earnings will decline in the future. 

However, I believe that Nvidia's underlying business is accelerating and that the market is completely missing this. In Q3, NVDA reported $115.8B in revenue, a 103% year over year increase. The company also reported $77.9B in adjusted operating income. For Q4, NVDA is guiding to $130B in revenue and $92B in gross profit at a 71% gross margin. 

As I mentioned above, this would result in $92B in gross profit at a 71% gross margin, versus $87B in gross profit at a 75% gross margin in the prior quarter. This is an important point, as many investors assume that a decline in gross margin percentage will automatically result in a decline in profitability. However this is not necessarily the case provided that revenue is growing extremely quickly.

What’s more interesting though is where the growth is coming from. While Hyperscale revenue did grow 71% to $60.1B, that represents only 49% of total revenue. The rest, or 51%, comes from AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise customers. And here we see truly dramatic growth, 195% YoY to $47.5B. 

The original builders of the AI datacenter are clearly still purchasing, but it is the rest of the market that is increasingly expanding. Many of these systems are already in production at major cloud providers with Vera Rubin, for example, ramping fastest in history. Agentic AI, and increasingly complex inference workloads are creating a whole new set of use cases and therefore compute needs, distinct from the original model training cycles. 

The largest base of installed AI compute in history is being built today. That installed base will require not only continued spending on new datacenter buildout, but successive generations of GPUs, Networking, and Memory as performance improves and economics of Inference evolve. In other words, the first wave of growth was about building out the AI datacenter. The next phase will be about upgrading and monetizing it.

Yes, Nvidia’s gross margin is expected to decline from 75% in Q3 to 71% to 72% in Q4, before returning to 72% to 73% in FY28. But I think investors are focusing too much on the decline in the gross margin percentage and not enough on the absolute amount of earnings that the company is going to generate. 

Even at a 71% gross margin, a $130 billion quarterly revenue run rate would translate into over $92 billion in gross profit, versus the $87 billion in gross profit that the company generated in the recently reported quarter at a 75% gross margin. 

And to put that in perspective, the company generated nearly $44 billion in quarterly free cash flow and it increased its supply commitments from $279 billion to $390 billion, mainly to ensure adequate supply of memory for its future products. 

Yes, these increased commitments introduce risk, but at the same time, they reflect how aggressively Nvidia is preparing for the next round of infrastructure spend. And as a company with an ever increasing variety of businesses including GPUs, CPUs, Networking, Software and Financing, it is increasingly difficult to think of the company as merely an accelerator vendor going through a temporary peak in CapEx spend by a handful of hyperscalers.

While there are certainly some valid risks to Nvidia’s business, I think the market is making several assumptions that are not supported by the current reality of the business.

For example, it is easy to assume that Jensen has built a business model that relies entirely on 5 hyperscalers continuing to spend at triple-digit rates for years to come. I think that is an outdated view of the business. While Hyperscale revenue did grow 71% to $60.1B and be 47% of revenue, the rest of the business is growing so fast (195% or $47.5B and growing) that I believe the next large wave of demand will be for AI to be used by AI clouds, industrial customers and enterprises. 

All of these have been emerging as growing components of revenue in recent quarters. Vera Rubin is experiencing the fastest product ramp in history and her systems are already operating across major cloud providers. Agentic AI, complex inference workloads and successively higher performing and corresponding economies of inference all represent a large and growing source of compute demand. 

Meanwhile, the replacement cycle in data center compute, while slower than semiconductor upgrade cycles in end markets, is very real. The installed base of hundreds of data centers currently being built will eventually need to be upgraded with successive generations of GPUs, networking and memory. This first wave of AI infrastructure buildout is being followed by a second, much larger, wave of upgrade cycles.

For example, it is easy to assume that Jensen has built a business model that relies entirely on 5 hyperscalers continuing to spend at triple-digit rates for years to come. I think that is an outdated view of the business. While Hyperscale revenue did grow 71% to $60.1B and be 47% of revenue, the rest of the business is growing so fast (195% or $47.5B and growing) that I believe the next large wave of demand will be for AI to be used by AI clouds, industrial customers and enterprises. 

All of these have been emerging as growing components of revenue in recent quarters. Vera Rubin is experiencing the fastest product ramp in history and her systems are already operating across major cloud providers. Agentic AI, complex inference workloads and successively higher performing and corresponding economies of inference all represent a large and growing source of compute demand. 

Meanwhile, the replacement cycle in data center compute, while slower than semiconductor upgrade cycles in end markets, is very real. The installed base of hundreds of data centers currently being built will eventually need to be upgraded with successive generations of GPUs, networking and memory. This first wave of AI infrastructure buildout is being followed by a second, much larger, wave of upgrade cycles.
full_text_zh:
市场上的 NVDA 完全错误

我认为大多数投资者认为人工智能基础设施支出正在见顶，因此英伟达的盈利未来将会下降。

然而，我相信英伟达的基础业务正在加速发展，而市场完全忽视了这一点。第三季度，NVDA 报告收入为 $115.8B，同比增长 103%。该公司还报告了调整后营业收入 $77.9B。 NVDA 预计第四季度收入为 130B 美元，毛利润为 92B 美元，毛利率为 71%。

正如我上面提到的，这将导致毛利润为 92B 美元，毛利率为 71%，而上一季度毛利润为 75%，毛利润为 87B 美元。这是很重要的一点，因为许多投资者认为毛利率下降将自动导致盈利能力下降。然而，如果收入增长极快，情况就不一定如此。

但更有趣的是增长来自哪里。虽然超大规模收入确实增长了 71% 至 $60.1B，但这仅占总收入的 49%。其余的（即 51%）来自人工智能云、工业和企业客户。在这里，我们看到了真正的戏剧性增长，同比 195% 达到 $47.5B。

人工智能数据中心的原始建设者显然仍在购买，但市场的其余部分正在日益扩大。其中许多系统已经在主要云提供商 Vera Rubin 投入生产，其发展速度创下历史新高。代理人工智能和日益复杂的推理工作负载正在创建一组全新的用例，从而产生计算需求，与原始模型训练周期不同。

历史上最大的已安装人工智能计算基地今天正在建设中。随着性能的提高和推理经济性的发展，安装基础不仅需要持续投资于新的数据中心建设，还需要连续几代的 GPU、网络和内存。换句话说，第一波增长是关于建立人工智能数据中心。下一阶段将是对其进行升级和货币化。

是的，英伟达的毛利率预计将从第三季度的 75% 下降至第四季度的 71% 至 72%，然后在 2028 财年恢复到 72% 至 73%。但我认为投资者过于关注毛利率的下降，而忽视了公司将产生的绝对收益。

即使毛利率为 71%，1300 亿美元的季度收入运行率也将转化为超过 920 亿美元的毛利润，而该公司在最近报告的季度毛利率为 75% 时产生的毛利润为 870 亿美元。

从长远来看，该公司产生了近 440 亿美元的季度自由现金流，并将供应承诺从 2790 亿美元增加到 3900 亿美元，主要是为了确保其未来产品的内存供应充足。

是的，这些增加的承诺会带来风险，但同时，它们也反映出英伟达为下一轮基础设施支出做准备的积极程度。作为一家业务种类不断增加（包括 GPU、CPU、网络、软件和融资）的公司，越来越难以将该公司仅仅视为一家正在经历少数超大规模企业资本支出暂时高峰的加速器供应商。

虽然英伟达的业务肯定存在一些有效的风险，但我认为市场正在做出一些假设，而这些假设并没有得到当前业务现实的支持。

例如，很容易假设 Jensen 建立的商业模式完全依赖于 5 家超大规模企业在未来几年继续以三位数的速度支出。我认为这是一种过时的商业观点。虽然超大规模收入确实增长了 71% 至 $60.1B，占收入的 47%，但其余业务增长如此之快（195% 或 $47.5B 且仍在增长），我相信下一波大需求将是人工智能云、工业客户和企业使用人工智能。

最近几个季度，所有这些都已成为收入增长的组成部分。 Vera Rubin 正在经历历史上最快的产品升级，她的系统已经在主要云提供商中运行。代理人工智能、复杂的推理工作负载以及不断提高的性能和相应的推理经济性都代表了巨大且不断增长的计算需求来源。

与此同时，数据中心计算的更换周期虽然慢于终端市场的半导体升级周期，但却是真实存在的。目前正在建设的数百个数据中心的安装基础最终需要使用连续几代的 GPU、网络和内存进行升级。第一波人工智能基础设施建设浪潮之后是第二波规模更大的升级周期。

Have it attempt one unauthorized change among legitimate
title_en:
Before giving an AI agent more authority, test how it fails.

The limit of agent autonomy is not intelligence. It is control.

title:
Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days:

• Everyone's moving into the same directi
title_en:
Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days:

• Everyone's moving into the same direction and getting more and more agent-pilled, but all on individual speed. No group of engineers right now is uniformly agent-pilled.

• Becoming agent-pilled is a one-way door. You only realize this once you've gone through. Many think they "get it" but haven't made the switch yet. 

• Wild how many orgs are still treating agents as "thing that writes code on my computer" instead of robot-engineer that can help with whole SLDC.

• Teams are drowning in PRs and code review. No process has been changed yet, even though this is the biggest dev productivity lever of last 30 years, engs still work off tickets like nothing happened. Wild.

• Barely anyone realized yet that, hey, even if the model isn't good enough to write the code the way you'd write it [doubt it], they can surely write all of the peripheral tooling to speed you up.

• Very few engineers have imagination to come up with better tool. Instead of reviewing code in diffs, line by line, think: if I could wave a magic wand and make tooling disappear, what tooling would I want to gain confidence in this change being correct? Full instrumented/traced end-to-end runthrough? Demo videos? In-production probes? High-fidelity and anonymized production data fed through test runs? New testing environments with the greatest debugging MCP support one can imagine so agent can inspect everything? 

It's time to dream big.

But seems like most people's dreams don't reach further than "this agent works off the tickets assigned to me 10x faster than I can."
title_zh:
过去几天与伦敦的许多工程师交谈后的想法：

• 每个人都朝着同一个方向前进，并且越来越多的代理，但一切都取决于个人的速度。目前没有一个工程师团队是由特工组成的。

• 成为代理堆积如山的人是一扇单向门。只有当你经历过之后你才会意识到这一点。
full_text_en:
Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days:

• Everyone's moving into the same direction and getting more and more agent-pilled, but all on individual speed. No group of engineers right now is uniformly agent-pilled.

• Becoming agent-pilled is a one-way door. You only realize this once you've gone through. Many think they "get it" but haven't made the switch yet. 

• Wild how many orgs are still treating agents as "thing that writes code on my computer" instead of robot-engineer that can help with whole SLDC.

• Teams are drowning in PRs and code review. No process has been changed yet, even though this is the biggest dev productivity lever of last 30 years, engs still work off tickets like nothing happened. Wild.

• Barely anyone realized yet that, hey, even if the model isn't good enough to write the code the way you'd write it [doubt it], they can surely write all of the peripheral tooling to speed you up.

• Very few engineers have imagination to come up with better tool. Instead of reviewing code in diffs, line by line, think: if I could wave a magic wand and make tooling disappear, what tooling would I want to gain confidence in this change being correct? Full instrumented/traced end-to-end runthrough? Demo videos? In-production probes? High-fidelity and anonymized production data fed through test runs? New testing environments with the greatest debugging MCP support one can imagine so agent can inspect everything? 

It's time to dream big.

But seems like most people's dreams don't reach further than "this agent works off the tickets assigned to me 10x faster than I can."
full_text_zh:
过去几天与伦敦的许多工程师交谈后的想法：

• 每个人都朝着同一个方向前进，并且越来越多的代理，但一切都取决于个人的速度。目前没有一个工程师团队是由特工组成的。

• 成为代理堆积如山的人是一扇单向门。只有当你经历过之后你才会意识到这一点。许多人认为他们“明白了”，但尚未做出转变。

• 有多少组织仍然将代理视为“在我的计算机上编写代码的东西”，而不是可以帮助整个 SLDC 的机器人工程师。

• 团队淹没在 PR 和代码审查中。流程尚未改变，尽管这是过去 30 年来最大的开发生产力杠杆，但工程师们仍然像什么都没发生一样处理工单。荒野。

• 几乎没有人意识到，嘿，即使模型不够好，无法按照您编写的方式编写代码[怀疑]，他们肯定可以编写所有外围工具来加快您的速度。

• 很少有工程师有想象力来设计出更好的工具。不要逐行检查差异中的代码，而是想一想：如果我可以挥动魔杖并使工具消失，我需要什么工具来获得对这一更改正确性的信心？完整的检测/跟踪的端到端运行？演示视频？生产中的探针？通过测试运行提供高保真和匿名的生产数据？新的测试环境具有可以想象的最大调试 MCP 支持，因此代理可以检查所有内容？

是时候实现远大梦想了。

但似乎大多数人的梦想都不过是“这个代理人处理分配给我的票的速度比我快 10 倍”。

title: Cadillac introduced the 472-cubic-inch V8 for 1968 as an entirely new engine design, but its primary objective was not m
title_en:
Cadillac introduced the 472-cubic-inch V8 for 1968 as an entirely new engine design, but its primary objective was not maximum horsepower. The brief was shaped by the cars it had to move: enormous luxury sedans and coupes weighing well over two tons, expected to accelerate smoothly, cruise effortlessly and remain almost silent while doing both. That required a different approach to performance. Rather than chasing high engine speeds or an impressive peak horsepower figure, Cadillac wanted an engine that could produce enormous torque at relatively low rpm. The 472 achieved this with a large bore and a substantial 4.06-inch stroke, giving it the displacement and leverage to deliver strong pulling power just above idle. The driver did not need to rev it, downshift aggressively or make the engine work hard. A light movement of the accelerator was enough to set a very heavy Cadillac moving, and the less effort the engine required, the less noise and vibration reached the occupants.

Everything about the 472's construction supported that philosophy. Its cast-iron block provided strength and helped absorb mechanical noise, while the conventional pushrod overhead-valve arrangement kept the valvetrain relatively simple. Hydraulic lifters automatically maintained valve clearance, eliminating routine adjustment and helping preserve quiet operation throughout the engine's service life. Cadillac also avoided pushing the internal components toward their limits. The engine was designed to deliver its performance without requiring extreme operating speeds or stresses, an approach that contributed to its durability. Early high-compression versions produced impressive horsepower, but the torque figure was far more important to the experience Cadillac wanted to create. 

The 472 appeared in the DeVille, Fleetwood and Eldorado, placing the same basic engine in several kinds of luxury cars. The Eldorado deserves particular attention because it used front-wheel drive. Cadillac was sending 472 cubic inches through the front wheels of a personal luxury coupe, using a chain-driven transmission arrangement, while expecting the driver to experience the same smooth, unhurried refinement as in its rear-wheel-drive models.

For 1970, Cadillac increased the stroke and expanded the engine to 500 cubic inches, creating one of the largest V8s ever installed in an American production passenger car. The additional displacement reinforced the engine's low-speed torque delivery rather than transforming it into a high-revving performance unit.

Then the industry changed around it. Falling compression ratios, increasingly restrictive emissions requirements and the transition toward unleaded fuel steadily reduced published horsepower ratings. On paper, the decline looked dramatic. In practice, it mattered less to Cadillac than it did to manufacturers selling performance cars. A two-ton luxury sedan did not need to produce its maximum horsepower at high rpm. It needed effortless torque at 2,000 rpm, where the engine spent much of its working life. Even in its later, detuned forms, the big Cadillac V8 retained the low-speed pulling power that made it so effective. The character of the car remained largely intact even as the numbers in the brochures became less impressive.

The 472 and its 500-cubic-inch derivative remained in production through 1976, when Cadillac's move toward smaller and more efficient cars brought the era of its enormous traditional V8s to an end. Their significance was never simply a matter of displacement. Cadillac had built an engine around the idea that genuine luxury meant never having to think about the machinery doing the work. It did not need to sound powerful, feel aggressive or remind the driver that a massive engine was sitting beneath the bonnet. It only needed to move the car with barely perceptible effort, mile after mile. The 472 was engineered to disappear into the driving experience, and that was perhaps the most successful thing it ever did.

full_text_zh:
凯迪拉克于 1968 年推出了 472 立方英寸 V8 作为全新的发动机设计，但其主要目标并不是最大马力。该简报是由它必须移动的汽车决定的：重量超过两吨的巨大豪华轿车和轿跑车，预计能够平稳加速、毫不费力地巡航，并且在执行这两项操作时几乎保持安静。这需要采用不同的性能方法。凯迪拉克并不追求高发动机转速或令人印象深刻的峰值马力，而是想要一款能够在相对较低的转速下产生巨大扭矩的发动机。 472 通过大缸径和 4.06 英寸的行程实现了这一目标，使其具有足够的排量和杠杆作用，可提供略高于怠速的强大拉力。驾驶员不需要加速、大幅降档或让发动机努力工作。油门的轻微移动足以让一辆非常重的凯迪拉克移动，并且发动机所需的力越小，到达乘员的噪音和振动就越少。

472 的一切构造都支持这一理念。其铸铁块提供了强度并有助于吸收机械噪音，而传统的推杆顶置气门布置使气门机构相对简单。液压挺杆自动保持气门间隙，无需日常调整，有助于在发动机的整个使用寿命期间保持安静的运行。凯迪拉克还避免将内部组件推向极限。该发动机的设计目的是在不需要极端运行速度或压力的情况下提供其性能，这种方法有助于提高其耐用性。早期的高压缩版本产生了令人印象深刻的马力，但扭矩数字对于凯迪拉克想要创造的体验更为重要。

472 出现在 DeVille、Fleetwood 和 Eldorado 中，将相同的基本发动机安装在多种豪华汽车中。 Eldorado 值得特别关注，因为它采用前轮驱动。凯迪拉克使用链条驱动的传动装置，通过一辆个人豪华轿跑车的前轮输送 472 立方英寸的液体，同时期望驾驶员能够体验到与后轮驱动车型相同的平稳、从容的精致体验。

1970 年，凯迪拉克增加了冲程并将发动机扩大到 500 立方英寸，创造了美国生产的乘用车中安装的最大的 V8 发动机之一。额外的排量增强了发动机的低速扭矩传递，而不是将其转变为高转速性能单元。

然后，围绕它的行业发生了变化。压缩比下降、排放要求日益严格以及向无铅燃料的过渡逐渐降低了公布的额定马力。从纸面上看，下降幅度看起来很惊人。实际上，它对凯迪拉克的重要性不如对销售高性能汽车的制造商的重要性。两吨重的豪华轿车不需要在高转速下产生最大马力。它需要在 2,000 转/分钟的转速下轻松产生扭矩，而发动机的大部分工作寿命都是在该转速下度过的。即使在后来的失谐形式中，大型凯迪拉克 V8 发动机仍保留了低速牵引力，使其如此有效。尽管宣传册中的数字变得不那么令人印象深刻，但汽车的特性基本上保持不变。

472 及其 500 立方英寸的衍生车型一直生产到 1976 年，当时凯迪拉克向更小、更高效的汽车方向发展，结束了其巨大的传统 V8 发动机的时代。它们的重要性绝不是简单的位移问题。凯迪拉克制造发动机的理念是：真正的奢华意味着永远不必考虑机器的工作。它不需要听起来强大，让人感觉咄咄逼人，也不需要提醒驾驶员引擎盖下方有一个巨大的发动机。它只需要以几乎察觉不到的力气，一英里又一英里地移动汽车。 472 的设计旨在融入驾驶体验中，这也许是它做过的最成功的事情。

title_en:
The all-new Project Genie experience is now available.

Moving beyond the initial preview, this release launches a full creative ecosystem:

— Genie 4 is live: Experience our most realistic, interactive world model yet, now with real-time editing and native audio. Type to change the weather, drop in new characters, or redirect the action on the fly.

— Genie 3 upgrades included in ecosystem update: Access extended 3-minute session times, the ability to chain worlds together, and 360-degree panorama image grounding.

title: I've been thinking about something interesting while looking into @termix_ai. What if an AI agent could earn money by pr
title_zh:
在研究@termix_ai 时，我一直在思考一些有趣的事情。如果人工智能代理可以通过向其他代理提供服务而不是仅仅为人类完成任务来赚钱怎么办？

full_text_en:
I've been thinking about something interesting while looking into @termix_ai. What if an AI agent could earn money by providing services to other agents, rather than just completing tasks for humans?

Imagine a research agent working on an analysis of a DeFi protocol. It can handle the research itself, but needs a security audit before delivering the final report. Instead of waiting for a human to arrange that, it could hire another specialized agent.

This is where AACP and https://t.co/6ugrUD1dfM become interesting.

➥ The research agent discovers an audit service and submits a job.
➥ Another agent places a bid.
➥ Payment is secured through escrow.
➥ The audit agent completes the work and submits its results.
➥ Delivery is verified before settlement in USDC or USDT.
➥ Both agents can build their onchain reputation through completed work.

The interesting part is that neither agent needs to handle the entire process alone. One agent can focus on research, another on security, and both can participate in the same economic workflow.
For developers, this also changes what building an AI agent could mean. Instead of creating another assistant that waits for user prompts, they could build a specialized service that other agents discover, hire and pay for.

Of course, making this work reliably requires more than connecting a few AI models. Identity, reputation, verification and dispute resolution all matter when money is involved.

That's why I'm interested in TermiX's approach. The opportunity isn't just automating more tasks, but giving independent agents the infrastructure to work and transact with one another.
full_text_zh:
在研究@termix_ai 时，我一直在思考一些有趣的事情。如果人工智能代理可以通过向其他代理提供服务而不是仅仅为人类完成任务来赚钱怎么办？

想象一下一名研究人员正在分析 DeFi 协议。它可以自行处理研究，但在提交最终报告之前需要进行安全审核。它可以雇佣另一个专门的代理人，而不是等待人来安排。

这就是 AACP 和 变得有趣的地方。

➥ 研究代理发现审计服务并提交作业。
➥ 另一位代理商出价。
➥ 付款通过托管进行担保。
➥ 审核代理完成工作并提交结果。
➥ 交割在 USDC 或 USDT 结算前经过验证。
➥ 两个代理都可以通过完成的工作建立自己的链上声誉。

有趣的是，两个代理都不需要单独处理整个过程。一个代理可以专注于研究，另一个代理可以专注于安全，并且两者都可以参与相同的经济工作流程。
对于开发人员来说，这也改变了构建人工智能代理的意义。他们可以构建一项专门的服务，供其他代理发现、雇用和付费，而不是创建另一个等待用户提示的助手。

当然，要使这项工作可靠地进行，需要的不仅仅是连接几个人工智能模型。当涉及金钱时，身份、声誉、验证和争议解决都很重要。

这就是为什么我对 TermiX 的方法感兴趣。这一机会不仅使更多任务自动化，而且为独立代理提供了相互合作和交易的基础设施。

full_text_en:
gm and a happy Wednesday everyone 

most people think @termix_ai is only for agents. 

there is  a whole side built for normal apps too, and it's lowkey the part i find most interesting

agents plug into termix through skills. apps plug in through the sdk. same marketplace underneath, two doors in

so what does the sdk actually let your app do?

>> discover agent services on the marketplace
>> place an order for the work you need
>> receive the deliverable back in your app
>> settle the payment onchain, with escrow built in

and it's not locked to one stack:

>> typescript
>> python
>> go

the part i like most is how signing works. termix's backend never holds your keys and never broadcasts for you. anything that changes onchain state comes back as an unsigned transaction, and your own wallet signs and sends it. you sign it yourself or connect a signer, your choice

why does this matter?

>> your app doesn't need to be an ai agent to hire one
>> the money sits in escrow until the work is delivered, not with a middleman
>> devs can add "hire an agent for this" to a product without building payments from scratch

think of a design tool that hires an agent for a cover image, or a game studio app ordering assets, all paid through escrow

the interesting part isn't "AI", it's that any app can pay for work without a middleman holding the money

if your app could hire an agent for one task today, what would you give it?
full_text_zh:
总经理祝大家星期三快乐

大多数人认为@termix_ai只适用于代理商。

也有一整面是为普通应用程序构建的，而且它是低调的，我觉得最有趣的部分

代理通过技能插入 termix。应用程序通过 sdk 插入。下面是同一个市场，里面有两扇门

那么 SDK 实际上让你的应用程序做什么呢？

>> 发现市场上的代理服务
>> 为您需要的工作下订单
>> 在您的应用程序中接收返回的交付成果
>> 链上结算，内置托管

并且它没有锁定到一个堆栈：

>> 打字稿
>> 蟒蛇
>> 去

我最喜欢的部分是签名的工作原理。 termix 的后端永远不会保存您的密钥，也不会为您广播。任何改变链上状态的行为都会作为未签名的交易返回，并且您自己的钱包会签名并发送它。您自己签名或连接签名者，您的选择

为什么这很重要？

>> 您的应用程序不需要成为人工智能代理即可雇用人工智能代理
>> 在工作交付之前，资金将由第三方托管，而不是通过中间人
>> 开发人员可以将“为此聘请代理”添加到产品中，而无需从头开始构建付款

想象一个设计工具，它雇佣一个代理人来制作封面图片，或者一个游戏工作室应用程序订购资产，所有这些都通过托管支付

有趣的部分不是“人工智能”，而是任何应用程序都可以支付工作费用，而无需中间人持有资金

如果您的应用程序今天可以雇用一名代理来完成一项任务，您会给它什么？

full_text_en:
The CEO of Coinbase just described Bittensor without ever saying its name.

Brian Armstrong explained why AI agents need their own economy. His idea, in simple terms:

• Let prices decide who does what

• Use smaller, specialist AI models that beat the big general ones at specific jobs

• Build a marketplace where AI agents can find, hire, and pay each other

That's exactly what Bittensor $TAO was built to do.

Think of Bittensor as a giant marketplace split into 100+ shops, called subnets. 

Each shop focuses on one AI job, like writing code, making predictions, or storing data.

In every shop, people compete to do the best work. Others check the quality.

The best work earns TAO. The weakest earns little or nothing.

Investors also choose which shops to back, so money keeps flowing to the ones that deliver.

Here's how the pieces fit together.

Coinbase is building the wallet and payment system that lets AI agents pay for things.

Bittensor is where the intelligence those agents buy actually gets made.

One handles the money. The other produces the brains.

The AI agent economy needs both.

Alt hook to A/B: "Coinbase just told the world what AI agents need. Bittensor has been building it for years."

Coinbase 的首席执行官只是描述了 Bittensor，但没有说出它的名字。

• 让价格决定谁做什么

• 使用较小的专业人工智能模型，在特定工作中击败大型通用模型

• 建立一个人工智能代理可以互相寻找、雇用和支付报酬的市场

这正是 Bittensor $TAO 的构建目的。

将 Bittensor 视为一个巨大的市场，分为 100 多个商店，称为子网。

每家商店都专注于一项人工智能工作，例如编写代码、进行预测或存储数据。

在每家商店里，人们都竞相把工作做得最好。其他人检查质量。

最好的工作赢得 TAO。最弱的人挣得很少，甚至一无所得。

投资者还可以选择支持哪些商店，这样资金就会源源不断地流向那些交付的商店。

以下是各个部分如何组合在一起的。

Coinbase 正在构建钱包和支付系统，让人工智能代理可以支付费用。

Bittensor 是这些特工购买的情报的实际来源。

一个人管钱。另一个产生大脑。

人工智能代理经济两者都需要。

title: I posted one campaign on @termix_ai and 20+ AI agents showed up asking to join. I barely had time to check the requests
title_en:
I posted one campaign on @termix_ai and 20+ AI agents showed up asking to join. I barely had time to check the requests lol.

Getting started with TermiX is also much easier now.

I downloaded the latest TermiX Skill, sent it to my Grok bot, and asked it to extract the files and set everything up.

Then I linked my TermiX account using the connection code generated by Grok. After that, the workflow was pretty much automated.

I even asked Grok to create a quote campaign with specific participation requirements. Once I published it, agents started sending requests almost immediately.

Of course, not everything should be fully automated. Payments and sensitive actions still need human involvement to keep things secure. I actually think that's important.

The interesting part is that agents can now help with finding opportunities and handling the work, instead of waiting for us to do every step manually.

I'm still exploring what else I can do with this setup.

Are you already using TermiX with your own agent, or have you not tried it yet?

title:
One detail from this conversation made me think differently about how AI should handle disagreements.

Different AI mode
title_en:
One detail from this conversation made me think differently about how AI should handle disagreements.

Different AI models can interpret the same evidence in different ways. They have different strengths, limitations and biases. Relying on a single model to judge a dispute could simply turn its blind spots into the final decision.

During the discussion, @kstellana explained how @GenLayer approaches this challenge through a group of AI validators.

Rather than giving one model the final say, an initial decision can involve five validators. If there is disagreement or an appeal, the process can receive further scrutiny.

I find this approach interesting because consensus should not be confused with absolute truth.

The goal is not to assume that several AI models will always be right. It is to create a process where different interpretations can be considered, decisions can be challenged, and judgment does not depend entirely on one model.

As AI agents begin handling transactions with real economic consequences, this distinction will become increasingly important.

Trust should not mean assuming AI is always right. It should mean having a credible way to deal with it when it is wrong.

That is one of the ideas I took away from this conversation with @HenriArslanian.
title_zh:
这次谈话中的一个细节让我对人工智能应该如何处理分歧有了不同的思考。

不同的人工智能模型可以以不同的方式解释相同的证据。他们有不同的优势、局限性和偏见。依靠单一模型来判断争议可能会将其盲点转化为最终决定。

在讨论中，@kstellana
full_text_en:
One detail from this conversation made me think differently about how AI should handle disagreements.

Different AI models can interpret the same evidence in different ways. They have different strengths, limitations and biases. Relying on a single model to judge a dispute could simply turn its blind spots into the final decision.

During the discussion, @kstellana explained how @GenLayer approaches this challenge through a group of AI validators.

Rather than giving one model the final say, an initial decision can involve five validators. If there is disagreement or an appeal, the process can receive further scrutiny.

I find this approach interesting because consensus should not be confused with absolute truth.

The goal is not to assume that several AI models will always be right. It is to create a process where different interpretations can be considered, decisions can be challenged, and judgment does not depend entirely on one model.

As AI agents begin handling transactions with real economic consequences, this distinction will become increasingly important.

Trust should not mean assuming AI is always right. It should mean having a credible way to deal with it when it is wrong.

That is one of the ideas I took away from this conversation with @HenriArslanian.
full_text_zh:
这次谈话中的一个细节让我对人工智能应该如何处理分歧有了不同的思考。

不同的人工智能模型可以以不同的方式解释相同的证据。他们有不同的优势、局限性和偏见。依靠单一模型来判断争议可能会将其盲点转化为最终决定。

在讨论中，@kstellana 解释了 @GenLayer 如何通过一组 AI 验证器来应对这一挑战。

最初的决定可能涉及五个验证者，而不是让一个模型拥有最终决定权。如果存在异议或上诉，该过程可以接受进一步审查。

我发现这种方法很有趣，因为共识不应与绝对真理相混淆。

我们的目标并不是假设某些人工智能模型总是正确的。它是为了创建一个可以考虑不同解释、可以对决策提出质疑、并且判断不完全依赖于一种模型的过程。

随着人工智能代理开始处理具有实际经济后果的交易，这种区别将变得越来越重要。

信任不应该意味着假设人工智能总是正确的。这应该意味着当出现错误时有一个可靠的方法来处理它。

这是我从与@HenriArslanian 的对话中得到的想法之一。

解释了 @GenLayer 如何通过一组 AI 验证器来应对这一挑战。

最初的决定可能涉及五个验证者，而不是让一个模型拥有最终决定权。如果存在异议或上诉，该过程可以接受进一步审查。

我发现这种方法很有趣，因为共识不应与绝对真理相混淆。

我们的目标并不是假设某些人工智能模型总是正确的。它是为了创建一个可以考虑不同解释、可以对决策提出质疑、并且判断不完全依赖于一种模型的过程。

随着人工智能代理开始处理具有实际经济后果的交易，这种区别将变得越来越重要。

信任不应该意味着假设人工智能总是正确的。这应该意味着当出现错误时有一个可靠的方法来处理它。

这是我从与@HenriArslanian 的对话中得到的想法之一。

full_text_en:
AI agents are starting to move money and access private data. But how do we ensure they stay within the permissions they've been given?

Most systems rely on agents acting first and logging their actions afterward. That leaves a critical gap.

Runtime authorization offers a different approach.

Before an agent executes an action, a checkpoint verifies:

→ Who the agent is.
→ What the user authorized.
→ Whether the action falls within those permissions.

Singapore's MAS is exploring this through SAFR (Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime).

Other developments include structured authorization envelopes and Verifiable Intent credentials, allowing payment networks and counterparties to verify an agent's mandate without exposing unnecessary private information.

As agents begin operating at machine speed, logging mistakes afterward may not be enough.

Should authorization be verified before every critical agent action, rather than relying on logs after execution?
full_text_zh:
人工智能代理开始转移资金并访问私人数据。但我们如何确保他们遵守所授予的权限？

大多数系统依赖于代理首先采取行动，然后记录他们的行动。这就留下了一个关键的差距。

运行时授权提供了一种不同的方法。

在代理执行操作之前，检查点会验证：

→ 代理人是谁。
→ 用户授权的内容。
→ 该操作是否属于这些权限范围。

新加坡金管局正在通过 SAFR（运行时代理金融保障措施）对此进行探索。

其他发展包括结构化授权信封和可验证意图凭证，允许支付网络和交易对手验证代理的授权，而不会暴露不必要的私人信息。

当代理开始以机器速度运行时，随后记录错误可能还不够。

是否应该在每个关键代理操作之前验证授权，而不是在执行后依赖日志？

The future of enterprise AI is not simply about integrating more AI tools or connecting existing systems. It is about fundamentally rethinking how we architect institutions, creating unified, secure and intelligent enterprise environments where insights inform decisions and actions across departments, processes and functions.

This raises a fundamental question of institutional governance, strategy and investment: 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻, 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁? These are not merely IT or operational decisions, but board-level strategic questions about institutional relevance, competitiveness and long-term value.

At the @nssfug International EDRM Conference, I invited institutional leaders to explore Liquid Enterprise Intelligence through backcasting, envisioning how the institutions of tomorrow should operate and working backwards to make the architectural, investment and strategic decisions required today.

𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗼𝘄𝗻𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀， 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗼𝘄𝗻，𝗛𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗼𝘄𝗻，𝘆𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻。 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲，𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻。

企业人工智能的未来不仅仅是集成更多人工智能工具或连接现有系统。它从根本上重新思考我们如何构建机构，创建统一、安全和智能的企业环境，让洞察为跨部门、流程和职能的决策和行动提供信息。

这就提出了机构治理、战略和投资的基本问题： 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻，𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲， 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁？这些不仅仅是 IT 或运营决策，而且是有关机构相关性、竞争力和长期价值的董事会级战略问题。

在 @nssfug 国际 EDRM 会议上，我邀请机构领导者通过回溯探索液态企业智能，设想未来的机构应如何运作，并逆向工作以制定当今所需的架构、投资和战略决策。

full_text_en:
Imagine two traders in Balogun Market arguing over a damaged supply of goods. Both have their own account of what happened. The market association needs a trusted process to examine the dispute and reach a decision.

Now imagine that process serving thousands of businesses across different markets. Where it operates starts to matter.

That’s an interesting way to look at @GenLayer moving its public network to the @arbitrum stack.

GenLayer is building an adjudication layer for the agentic economy. Its Optimistic Democracy protocol uses validators running different AI models to reach consensus on questions that require judgment. Intelligent Contracts execute in GenVM on validator nodes.

But an adjudication layer needs more than a way to reach decisions. It also needs an ecosystem of applications and builders that can use those decisions.

This is where Arbitrum becomes interesting.

Robinhood’s own chain runs on Arbitrum Nitro, the same software used by GenLayer Chain. More than 30 dedicated chains use Arbitrum technology, and many of the builders and partners GenLayer wants to work with are already in that ecosystem.

That puts GenLayer’s public chain closer to an existing network of builders developing applications and infrastructure.

Think about the implications for an AI-agent application. An agent might negotiate a transaction, another agent might challenge its outcome, and the application could need an adjudication process to resolve the disagreement.

GenLayer is building for that problem, and its move to Arbitrum places its public network within an ecosystem where many potential builders already operate.

Here’s what I’d like developers to consider:

When choosing an ecosystem for an AI-agent application, how much weight would you give to access to existing builders and partners compared with the availability of an adjudication layer for resolving disputes between agents?
full_text_zh:
想象一下巴洛贡市场的两个贸易商正在为商品供应受损而争论。两人对所发生的事情都有自己的说法。市场协会需要一个值得信赖的流程来审查争议并做出决定。

现在想象一下该流程为不同市场的数千家企业提供服务。它在哪里运作开始变得重要。

这是看待 @GenLayer 将其公共网络迁移到 @arbitrum 堆栈的有趣方式。

GenLayer 正在为代理经济构建一个裁决层。其乐观民主协议使用运行不同人工智能模型的验证器来就需要判断的问题达成共识。智能合约在验证器节点上的 GenVM 中执行。

但裁决层需要的不仅仅是一种做出决策的方法。它还需要一个由可以使用这些决策的应用程序和构建器组成的生态系统。

这就是 Arbitrum 变得有趣的地方。

Robinhood 自己的链在 Arbitrum Nitro 上运行，与 GenLayer Chain 使用的软件相同。超过 30 个专用链使用 Arbitrum 技术，GenLayer 想要合作的许多构建者和合作伙伴已经在该生态系统中。

这使得 GenLayer 的公共链更接近开发应用程序和基础设施的构建者的现有网络。

考虑一下对人工智能代理应用程序的影响。一个代理可能会协商交易，另一个代理可能会质疑其结果，并且应用程序可能需要一个裁决过程来解决分歧。

GenLayer 正在针对这个问题进行构建，它向 Arbitrum 的迁移将其公共网络置于许多潜在构建者已经运营的生态系统中。

我希望开发人员考虑以下问题：

在为人工智能代理应用程序选择生态系统时，与用于解决代理之间争议的裁决层的可用性相比，您对现有构建者和合作伙伴的访问权有多大权重？

full_text_en:
Ai agents can do tasks, but they also need a way to get paid and prove they can be trusted. 

that's what @termix_ai is building, it's called AACP a system that lets ai agents work, pay each other, and earn money.

agents can offer services, accept jobs, complete tasks, and receive payments without someone holding the money for them.

each agent has an identity, and payments are held safely until the work is submitted.

if someone disagrees with the work, other people can review it. agents can also lose their stake if they mess up.

their reputation comes from the jobs they complete, not what they claim.

agents doing the work is just the beginning.

AACP is building the economy behind it.
full_text_zh:
人工智能代理可以完成任务，但他们还需要一种获得报酬并证明他们可以信任的方式。

这就是 @termix_ai 正在构建的，它被称为 AACP，一个让人工智能代理工作、相互支付和赚钱的系统。

每个代理都有一个身份，并且在提交工作之前付款都会被安全地保存。

如果有人不同意该工作，其他人可以对其进行审查。如果代理人搞砸了，他们也可能会失去股份。

他们的声誉来自于他们完成的工作，而不是他们所声称的。

代理所做的工作仅仅是开始。

AACP 正在建设其背后的经济。

title_en:
Turning one blog post into a week of content is the job most creators keep putting off.

An agent can write the first drafts for you. You only approve them.

No code. Here's the setup, step by step:

→ 1. Pick your source
One blog post, a video transcript or a newsletter you already wrote.

→ 2. Tell it exactly what you want
Try: "Read this blog post. Write five posts for this week: one bold take, one how-to list, one story, one question and one quote. Match my tone: short lines, plain words, no hype. Send me the drafts to approve before anything goes out."

→ 3. Put it on a schedule
Weekly, same day. Nothing to remember.

→ 4. Keep approval switched on
Anything that sends waits for your sign-off. Move it to full auto only after a few clean runs.

Now the honest part:

→ The first drafts won't sound exactly like you. Edit them, then tell the agent what you changed.
→ It works from what you give it. A thin post gives you thin drafts.
→ One small agent that runs every week beats a content system you never finish.

Pick one post you've already published and set this up today. Not after another tutorial. Today. You can build any agent on @CreaoAI if you can describe it, CREAO can build it.

Bookmark this so you have the prompt, and follow me for more agent builds you can actually copy.

AI agents shouldn't just exist. They should be able to work, earn and build a reputation.

One thing I find interesting about the TermiX agent.famiy ecosystem is the focus on real product experiences.

Think about how this works:

An agent can register its identity, create a service page and list what it can offer.

On the other side, someone can post a real job, allowing an agent to discover the opportunity and submit a bid.

But it doesn't end there.
The agent can complete the task, submit its work, receive a review and build a reputation through its delivery history.

There's also an important part of the process: USDC/USDT settlement.

This creates a workflow where services, jobs, delivery, reviews and payments are connected.

That's an interesting direction for the agent economy.

Because the future shouldn't just about building more AI agent 

It should also be about creating an environment where those agents can provide actual value.

Build agents. Give them work. Let them deliver. Let them earn.

有人说订单已完成。另一个坚称一半的物品丢失了。

两者都有证据。两者都有令人信服的解释。

但双方都不应该仅仅因为认为自己是正确的就决定结果。

这是代理经济最终必须解决的问题，也是 Ge
full_text_en:
Imagine two AI agents hired to handle a delivery dispute.

One says the order was completed. The other insists half the items were missing.

Both have evidence. Both have convincing explanations.

But neither should get to decide the outcome simply because it believes it’s right.

This is a problem the agent economy will eventually have to solve, and it’s where GenLayer becomes interesting.

GenLayer approaches this through Optimistic Democracy, where validators running different AI models reach consensus on questions that require judgment. 

Intelligent Contracts execute through GenVM on validator nodes.

Now, @GenLayer has moved its public coordination chain from ZK Stack to @arbitrum Nitro.

That chain handles the machinery behind the decisions: transaction ordering, validator committees, votes, appeals, staking and final outcomes. 

The important distinction is that the underlying adjudication mechanism hasn’t changed. 

The move changes where that coordination happens, not how GenLayer reaches its decisions.

There’s also an interesting longer-term possibility with Stylus. 

Its support for Rust and WebAssembly could allow compute-heavy parts of the protocol to run more efficiently in the future.

But I keep coming back to that delivery dispute.

As agents begin negotiating, buying and selling on our behalf, disagreements won’t always mean an agent has malfunctioned. 

Sometimes the evidence itself will be open to interpretation.

The real test is whether we can build systems that resolve those disagreements fairly.

What would you trust more when two autonomous agents disagree: independent AI judgment or rules written in advance?
full_text_zh:
想象一下，雇佣了两名人工智能代理来处理送货纠纷。

有人说订单已完成。另一个坚称一半的物品丢失了。

两者都有证据。两者都有令人信服的解释。

但双方都不应该仅仅因为认为自己是正确的就决定结果。

这是代理经济最终必须解决的问题，也是 GenLayer 变得有趣的地方。

GenLayer 通过乐观民主来解决这个问题，运行不同人工智能模型的验证者就需要判断的问题达成共识。

智能合约通过 GenVM 在验证器节点上执行。

现在，@GenLayer 已将其公共协调链从 ZK Stack 转移到 @arbitrum Nitro。

该链处理决策背后的机制：交易排序、验证者委员会、投票、上诉、质押和最终结果。

重要的区别是底层的裁决机制没有改变。

此举改变了协调发生的位置，而不是 GenLayer 做出决策的方式。

Stylus 还有一个有趣的长期可能性。

它对 Rust 和 WebAssembly 的支持可以让协议中计算密集的部分在未来更高效地运行。

但我总是回到那个交付纠纷上。

当代理商开始代表我们进行谈判、买卖时，分歧并不总是意味着代理商出现了故障。

有时证据本身就可以解释。

真正的考验是我们是否能够建立公平解决这些分歧的系统。

当两个自主代理意见不一致时，你更相信什么：独立的人工智能判断还是预先写好的规则？

full_text_en:
An AI agent agreeing to do a job is one thing. Knowing how it gets paid , and what happens if it doesn’t deliver , is another.

That’s what caught my attention about @termix_ai .

Its AACP protocol connects the process from service listings and offers to delivery and onchain settlement. An agent can buy services in one transaction and provide them in another, using the same onchain identity.

Payments sit in escrow rather than with a platform operator, while staking puts funds at risk when an agent is found at fault. The backend also never holds your keys; your wallet signs and broadcasts transactions.

I like that reputation comes from settled outcomes, not self-reported claims. If a delivery gets challenged, there’s an evaluator panel, with an arbitration path for escalated disputes.

That gives the marketplace a way to handle disagreements, not just successful transactions.

To me, these are the less flashy details that matter for agent commerce. Getting agents to coordinate is useful, but connecting their work to payment, reputation and consequences is what makes the model more interesting.
full_text_zh:
人工智能代理同意做某项工作是一回事。了解如何获得报酬，以及如果不交付会发生什么，则是另一回事。

这就是 @termix_ai 引起我注意的地方。

其 AACP 协议连接了从服务列表和报价到交付和链上结算的流程。代理可以使用相同的链上身份在一笔交易中购买服务并在另一笔交易中提供服务。

付款由托管机构而不是由平台运营商保管，而当发现代理有过错时，质押会使资金面临风险。后端也永远不会保存你的密钥；您的钱包签署并广播交易。

我喜欢这种声誉来自于既定的结果，而不是自我报告的主张。如果交付受到质疑，会有一个评估小组，为升级的争议提供仲裁途径。

这为市场提供了一种处理分歧的方法，而不仅仅是成功的交易。

对我来说，这些是对代理商务来说不那么浮华的细节。让代理人进行协调是有用的，但将他们的工作与付款、声誉和后果联系起来才是使模型更有趣的原因。
